# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium. Once considered a rare and uniformly fatal disease, CA is increasingly recognized as an underdiagnosed cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), aortic stenosis, and unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy [1,2]. Advances in noninvasive imaging and the advent of disease-modifying therapies have transformed CA from a diagnosis of exclusion into a treatable condition [3].

## Epidemiology and Classification

The two principal forms responsible for the majority of CA are immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) amyloidosis and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis [4]. AL amyloidosis arises from a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia producing misfolded light chains, with an estimated incidence of 9–14 cases per million person-years [5]. ATTR amyloidosis results from deposition of transthyretin, either in its wild-type form (ATTRwt), predominantly affecting elderly men, or in hereditary form (ATTRv) caused by pathogenic *TTR* gene variants [6]. Autopsy studies and imaging series suggest ATTRwt is present in up to 13% of patients with HFpEF and a substantial proportion of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement [7,8].

## Pathophysiology

Amyloid fibril deposition increases myocardial stiffness, producing restrictive physiology, diastolic dysfunction, and ultimately systolic impairment [9]. In AL amyloidosis, circulating light chains exert direct cardiotoxicity through oxidative stress and impaired cellular function, partly explaining the disproportionately poor prognosis relative to amyloid burden [10]. In ATTR, destabilization of the tetrameric transthyretin protein leads to monomer dissociation, misfolding, and aggregation [11].

## Clinical Presentation

Patients typically present with progressive heart failure, fatigue, and exertional dyspnea [12]. Extracardiac clues are valuable: bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, and biceps tendon rupture frequently precede ATTR cardiac involvement by years [13]. Periorbital purpura and macroglossia are characteristic of AL amyloidosis [4]. Conduction system disease, atrial fibrillation, and low-voltage electrocardiograms despite increased wall thickness are common findings [14].

## Diagnosis

A high index of suspicion is essential. Echocardiography may reveal increased ventricular wall thickness, biatrial enlargement, and a characteristic apical-sparing pattern of longitudinal strain ("cherry-on-top") [15]. Cardiac magnetic resonance demonstrates diffuse late gadolinium enhancement and elevated extracellular volume, reflecting interstitial expansion [16]. A landmark advance was the recognition that bone-avid radiotracer scintigraphy (technetium-labeled pyrophosphate or DPD) can diagnose ATTR-CA noninvasively with high sensitivity and specificity [17]. Importantly, the diagnosis of ATTR by scintigraphy requires exclusion of a monoclonal protein via serum free light-chain assay and serum/urine immunofixation, as AL amyloidosis can also show tracer uptake [18]. Endomyocardial biopsy remains the gold standard when noninvasive criteria are not met, with mass spectrometry enabling definitive amyloid typing [19]. Genetic testing is recommended in all patients with confirmed ATTR to distinguish hereditary from wild-type disease [6].

## Treatment

Management of AL amyloidosis targets the underlying plasma cell clone. Bortezomib-based regimens, and more recently the addition of daratumumab, have improved hematologic and organ responses [20,21]. Autologous stem cell transplantation remains an option for selected, eligible patients [22]. Early diagnosis is critical, as advanced cardiac involvement portends a median survival of less than six months without effective therapy [10].

For ATTR-CA, transthyretin stabilizers represent a major therapeutic milestone. The ATTR-ACT trial demonstrated that tafamidis reduced all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in patients with ATTR-CA [23]. More recently, acoramidis, another stabilizer, showed clinical benefit in the ATTRibute-CM trial [24]. Gene-silencing therapies, including the small interfering RNA agents patisiran and vutrisiran, and the antisense oligonucleotide inotersen, reduce hepatic transthyretin production [25,26]. The HELIOS-B trial demonstrated that vutrisiran reduced mortality and cardiovascular events in ATTR-CA [27]. Emerging approaches include CRISPR-based in vivo gene editing, which produced durable reductions in serum transthyretin in early-phase studies [28].

Supportive heart failure management relies on cautious diuresis; conventional neurohormonal agents are often poorly tolerated owing to hypotension and the restrictive physiology [29]. Anticoagulation is warranted in atrial fibrillation given high thromboembolic risk [14]. Selected patients with end-stage disease may be candidates for cardiac or combined organ transplantation [30].

## Conclusion

Cardiac amyloidosis has shifted from an underrecognized terminal diagnosis to an actively managed disease. Heightened clinical awareness, leveraging extracardiac red flags and noninvasive imaging, enables earlier diagnosis when therapies are most effective [2,17]. With multiple disease-modifying agents now available and novel gene-editing strategies on the horizon, the prognosis for patients with CA continues to improve. Future priorities include refining screening strategies, optimizing combination therapy, and ensuring equitable access to costly treatments [3,23].
